title: Judges 20:18–28
context: Israel inquires of God at Bethel, where the ark and Phinehas the priest were at that time, and receives answers, yet suffers two heavy defeats before a third inquiry brings the promise of victory. The text does not explain why God allowed the first two defeats, and readers should be cautious about filling that silence. Some observe that Israel first asked only who should go up first, not whether to fight, and that their questions grow humbler as they weep, fast and offer sacrifices; others suggest the whole nation was being humbled for its own condition. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly agree that God remains sovereign and just even when his purposes are not explained, and that the passage calls for humility rather than confident speculation. No doctrinal division turns on these verses.

verses.text: The children of Israel arose, went up to Bethel, and asked counsel of God. They asked, “Who shall go up for us first to battle against the children of Benjamin?” The LORD said, “Judah first.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Israel asks God who should go up first, not whether they should fight at all. The LORD answers that Judah should go first.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God answering the question asked, while the text leaves unstated why the larger question was not raised. Readers in both traditions commonly observe the form of the question without claiming certainty about Israel’s motives.

verses.text: The children of Israel rose up in the morning and encamped against Gibeah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel encamping against Gibeah with confidence after receiving an answer. The narrative moves quickly toward battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the answer about Judah does not promise victory. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a sequence in which outcomes will surprise the Israelites.

verses.text: The men of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin; and the men of Israel set the battle in array against them at Gibeah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the men of Israel arraying themselves for battle at Gibeah. Their numbers and their just cause lead them to expect a straightforward victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confident deployment as preparing for an unexpected reversal. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as narrative setup rather than a theological statement.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin came out of Gibeah, and on that day destroyed twenty-two thousand of the Israelite men down to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the shocking loss of twenty-two thousand Israelites on the first day. The text does not explain why God allowed this defeat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the silence of the text about God’s reasons. Both traditions commonly urge humility here, acknowledging that God’s purposes are not always disclosed (compare Deuteronomy 29:29).

verses.text: The people, the men of Israel, encouraged themselves, and set the battle again in array in the place where they set themselves in array the first day.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Israelites encouraging themselves and preparing again for battle. Their resolve remains, though shaken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that their encouragement comes from themselves before they turn again to the LORD in the next verse. Readers in both traditions commonly observe this order without pressing it into a firm explanation.

verses.text: The children of Israel went up and wept before the LORD until evening; and they asked of the LORD, saying, “Shall I again draw near to battle against the children of Benjamin my brother?” The LORD said, “Go up against him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel weeping before the LORD and asking whether to fight their brother again. Their question now includes the word brother, showing growing grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the deeper humility in this second inquiry, which asks whether to go up at all. The LORD says to go up, and both traditions commonly read his answer as permission, not a promise of victory.

verses.text: The children of Israel came near against the children of Benjamin the second day.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Israel drawing near for battle on the second day. They act on the word they received, even after the painful losses of the first day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see their obedience to God’s answer as genuine. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for another painful outcome.

verses.text: Benjamin went out against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed down to the ground of the children of Israel again eighteen thousand men. All these drew the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel losing eighteen thousand more men on the second day. Obedience to God’s word does not guarantee immediate success.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s purposes as not immediately clear in the second defeat. Both traditions commonly resist confident explanations, while noting that the defeats lead Israel to deeper humility in the next verse.

verses.text: Then all the children of Israel and all the people went up, and came to Bethel, and wept, and sat there before the LORD, and fasted that day until evening; then they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see all the people going to Bethel to weep, sit before the LORD, fast and offer sacrifices. Their response now shows wholehearted humility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burnt offerings and peace offerings as seeking reconciliation with God. Readers in both traditions commonly see this as the most complete turning to God in the chapter.

verses.text: The children of Israel asked the LORD (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the parenthetical explanation that the ark of the covenant was at Bethel in those days. The narrator provides background for the inquiry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the presence of the ark as marking the inquiry as a formal seeking of God’s will. Both traditions commonly note that this detail places the story early in Israel’s history in the land.

verses.text: and Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, stood before it in those days), saying, “Shall I yet again go out to battle against the children of Benjamin my brother, or shall I cease?” The LORD said, “Go up; for tomorrow I will deliver him into your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, stood before the ark, placing the story in the generation after Joshua (compare Numbers 25:7). This time the LORD promises victory the next day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inquiry now asking whether to fight or cease, and God answering with a clear promise. Readers in both traditions commonly see a move from self-confidence to humility before God’s word is given in full.
